traps.snippet:
IF OBJECT_ID('tempdb..#claims') IS NOT NULL DROP TABLE #claims;

        SELECT  c.claim_id,
                c.claim_number,
                c.policy_id,
                c.customer_id,
                c.lob_code,
                c.loss_date,
                c.reported_date,
                p.policy…
traps.note: The #claims temp table holds the claims enriched with policy and customer data; in Spark it becomes a DataFrame.

DATEADD(MONTH,-12,@AsOfDate) only clamps to a month-end when it has to. Spark add_months also moves a month-end input to a month-end, so @AsOfDate = 2025-02-28 gives 2024-02-29 instead of 2024-02-28 and the 12-month window changes. Latent: only month-end reporting dates trigger it.

traps.snippet:
IF OBJECT_ID('tempdb..#flags') IS NOT NULL DROP TABLE #flags;

        SELECT  f.*,
                f.early_notification_flag + f.invalid_reg_flag
                  + f.new_customer_flag + f.lob_mismatch_flag     AS fraud_score
        INTO    #flags
traps.note: The #flags temp table holds the indicator flags and score; in Spark it becomes a DataFrame.

lob_code is VARCHAR(5). Under the CI collation, 'mot' and 'Mot' match 'MOT', so those claims get the motor registration check; a plain Spark equality would skip them. The later UPPER() suggests mixed-case values really exist.
lob_code is VARCHAR(5), and the RTRIM at line 140 shows it can carry trailing spaces. 'MOT ' = 'MOT' in SQL Server but not in Spark.

The LIKE pattern uses the [0-9] and [A-Z] character classes, and [A-Z] is case-insensitive under the CI collation. Spark LIKE would read them as literal text, so it must become an rlike with case-insensitive letters.
The <> compares text with text: a substring of policy_number (VARCHAR) against lob_code (VARCHAR). Under the CI collation, a case difference such as 'mot' vs 'MOT' is not a mismatch; in Spark it is.
SQL Server ignores trailing spaces when comparing, so a lob_code of 'MOT ' equals the 3-character prefix 'MOT'. Spark would raise the mismatch flag.
SUBSTRING(policy_number, 0, 4) returns only 3 characters in T-SQL. Spark substring(x, 0, 4) returns 4, which would change every lob_mismatch_flag.
CONVERT style 112 gives yyyymmdd and needs date_format 'yyyyMMdd'. A plain cast would give yyyy-MM-dd, which also breaks the CHAR(8) key.
CONVERT style 103 gives dd/mm/yyyy in the reason text and needs date_format 'dd/MM/yyyy'. A string cast would give yyyy-MM-dd.

contracts.grain: One row per claim reported in the 12 months up to the reporting date (@AsOfDate), with its SIU fraud flags, score and referral band.

columns.name: policy_number
columns.description: Taken from the latest policy snapshot on or before @AsOfDate. It can be NULL if the policy is not in that snapshot (none are NULL in this output).

columns.name: lob_code
columns.description: The claim's lob_code, upper-cased and with trailing spaces removed.

columns.name: early_notification_flag
columns.description: 1 when the claim was reported 0-30 days after the policy's EXPIRY date. The comment says the start of cover is meant, but the legacy code uses expiry_date, so the migration must do the same. 0 when that date is NULL.

columns.name: invalid_reg_flag
columns.description: 1 for MOT claims whose vehicle_reg doesn't match the T-SQL pattern [0-9][0-9]%-[A-Z]%-[0-9]%. 0 when vehicle_reg is NULL (because comparing to NULL gives UNKNOWN).

columns.name: new_customer_flag
columns.description: 1 when loss_date minus customer_since is under 180 days. 0 when customer_since is NULL.

columns.name: lob_mismatch_flag
columns.description: 1 when SUBSTRING(policy_number,0,4) (which gives the first 3 characters) differs from the raw claim lob_code. 0 when policy_number is NULL.

columns.name: fraud_score
columns.description: The sum of the four flags, from 0 to 4.

columns.name: fraud_band
columns.description: HIGH if the score is 2 or more, MEDIUM if it is 1, LOW if it is 0.

columns.name: reason_text
columns.description: 'Notified dd/mm/yyyy' (style 103), then ' - no indicators' or ' -' followed by the tokens EARLY/REG/NEWCUST/LOB for each flag set.

columns.name: as_of_date
columns.description: The @AsOfDate run parameter. It is the same for every row.

defects.title: Early notification measured from policy expiry instead of inception
defects.description: early_notification_flag is set when DATEDIFF(DAY, expiry_date, reported_date) is between 0 and 30, i.e. the claim was reported within 30 days AFTER the policy expired. A claim cannot normally be reported 0-30 days after expiry under live cover, so the flag almost never fires for genuine early claims and fires wrongly for claims reported just after expiry. fraud_score, fraud_band and reason_text follow from it.
defects.intended_behaviour: Per the comment 'claim notified within 30 days of the cover starting' (CR-0954): DATEDIFF(DAY, inception_date, reported_date) BETWEEN 0 AND 30.
defects.impact_query: WITH snap AS (SELECT MAX(snapshot_date) AS sd FROM stg_policy_snapshots WHERE snapshot_date <= DATE'2025-12-31'), p AS (SELECT ps.policy_id, MAX(ps.inception_date) AS inception_date FROM stg_policy_snapshots ps JOIN snap ON ps.snapshot_date = snap.sd GROUP BY ps.policy_id) SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected FROM golden_rpt_claim_fraud_flags g LEFT JOIN p ON p.policy_id = g.policy_id WHERE g.early_notification_flag <> CASE WHEN datediff(g.reported_date, p.inception_date) BETWEEN 0 AND 30 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END

impact.query: WITH snap AS (SELECT MAX(snapshot_date) AS sd FROM stg_policy_snapshots WHERE snapshot_date <= DATE'2025-12-31'), p AS (SELECT ps.policy_id, MAX(ps.inception_date) AS inception_date FROM stg_policy_snapshots ps JOIN snap ON ps.snapshot_date = snap.sd GROUP BY ps.policy_id) SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected FROM golden_rpt_claim_fraud_flags g LEFT JOIN p ON p.policy_id = g.policy_id WHERE g.early_notification_flag <> CASE WHEN datediff(g.reported_date, p.inception_date) BETWEEN 0 AND 30 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END

defects.title: Policies missing from the single latest snapshot get blank details and silently score 0
defects.description: Every claim is joined to the one global MAX(snapshot_date) on or before the as-of date. If a claim's policy is not in that extract (lapsed or cancelled, or the extract is incomplete), the LEFT JOIN returns NULL policy_number, inception and expiry dates and vehicle_reg. The early, registration and line-of-business indicators then all evaluate to 0, because NULL comparisons are unknown, and nothing shows that the checks could not be made.
defects.intended_behaviour: Use each policy's latest snapshot on or before the reporting date (CR-1529), or at least flag claims whose policy details are missing, rather than scoring them as clean.
defects.impact_query: WITH snap AS (SELECT MAX(snapshot_date) AS sd FROM stg_policy_snapshots WHERE snapshot_date <= DATE'2025-12-31'), cur AS (SELECT DISTINCT ps.policy_id FROM stg_policy_snapshots ps JOIN snap ON ps.snapshot_date = snap.sd), anyp AS (SELECT DISTINCT policy_id FROM stg_policy_snapshots WHERE snapshot_date <= DATE'2025-12-31') SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected FROM golden_rpt_claim_fraud_flags g JOIN anyp a ON a.policy_id = g.policy_id LEFT JOIN cur c ON c.policy_id = g.policy_id WHERE c.policy_id IS NULL

impact.query: WITH snap AS (SELECT MAX(snapshot_date) AS sd FROM stg_policy_snapshots WHERE snapshot_date <= DATE'2025-12-31'), cur AS (SELECT DISTINCT ps.policy_id FROM stg_policy_snapshots ps JOIN snap ON ps.snapshot_date = snap.sd), anyp AS (SELECT DISTINCT policy_id FROM stg_policy_snapshots WHERE snapshot_date <= DATE'2025-12-31') SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected FROM golden_rpt_claim_fraud_flags g JOIN anyp a ON a.policy_id = g.policy_id LEFT JOIN cur c ON c.policy_id = g.policy_id WHERE c.policy_id IS NULL

defects.title: Six-month new-customer window hard-coded as 180 days
defects.description: new_customer_flag uses DATEDIFF(DAY, customer_since, loss_date) < 180. Six calendar months is 181-184 days, so customers whose loss falls in the last few days of their first six months are not flagged.
defects.intended_behaviour: Flag when loss_date < DATEADD(MONTH, 6, customer_since), i.e. customer for less than six calendar months at the date of loss.
defects.impact_query: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected FROM golden_rpt_claim_fraud_flags g LEFT JOIN dw_dim_customer dc ON dc.customer_id = g.customer_id WHERE g.new_customer_flag <> CASE WHEN g.loss_date < add_months(dc.customer_since, 6) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END

impact.query: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected FROM golden_rpt_claim_fraud_flags g LEFT JOIN dw_dim_customer dc ON dc.customer_id = g.customer_id WHERE g.new_customer_flag <> CASE WHEN g.loss_date < add_months(dc.customer_since, 6) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END

defects.title: LOB mismatch compares only the first 3 characters of the policy number
defects.description: SUBSTRING(policy_number, 0, 4) in T-SQL returns only the first 3 characters. Any line-of-business code longer than 3 characters (lob_code is VARCHAR(5)) can never equal its policy-number prefix, so every such claim is wrongly flagged as a mismatch.
defects.intended_behaviour: Compare the full prefix before the first '/' of the policy number (e.g. MOT in MOT/2024/500001) with the trimmed, upper-cased lob_code.
defects.impact_query: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected FROM golden_rpt_claim_fraud_flags g WHERE g.policy_number IS NOT NULL AND g.lob_mismatch_flag <> CASE WHEN upper(substring_index(g.policy_number, '/', 1)) <> upper(trim(g.lob_code)) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END

impact.query: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected FROM golden_rpt_claim_fraud_flags g WHERE g.policy_number IS NOT NULL AND g.lob_mismatch_flag <> CASE WHEN upper(substring_index(g.policy_number, '/', 1)) <> upper(trim(g.lob_code)) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END

defects.title: Motor claims with a missing registration are not flagged
defects.description: For motor claims, vehicle_reg NOT LIKE pattern is unknown when vehicle_reg is NULL, so invalid_reg_flag = 0. A missing registration is treated as valid.
defects.intended_behaviour: A motor claim with no registration should count as not being in the Irish format (flag = 1).
defects.impact_query: WITH snap AS (SELECT MAX(snapshot_date) AS sd FROM stg_policy_snapshots WHERE snapshot_date <= DATE'2025-12-31'), p AS (SELECT ps.policy_id, MAX(ps.vehicle_reg) AS vehicle_reg FROM stg_policy_snapshots ps JOIN snap ON ps.snapshot_date = snap.sd GROUP BY ps.policy_id) SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected FROM golden_rpt_claim_fraud_flags g LEFT JOIN p ON p.policy_id = g.policy_id WHERE upper(trim(g.lob_code)) = 'MOT' AND g.invalid_reg_flag = 0 AND p.vehicle_reg IS NULL

impact.query: WITH snap AS (SELECT MAX(snapshot_date) AS sd FROM stg_policy_snapshots WHERE snapshot_date <= DATE'2025-12-31'), p AS (SELECT ps.policy_id, MAX(ps.vehicle_reg) AS vehicle_reg FROM stg_policy_snapshots ps JOIN snap ON ps.snapshot_date = snap.sd GROUP BY ps.policy_id) SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected FROM golden_rpt_claim_fraud_flags g LEFT JOIN p ON p.policy_id = g.policy_id WHERE upper(trim(g.lob_code)) = 'MOT' AND g.invalid_reg_flag = 0 AND p.vehicle_reg IS NULL

tests.description: Claims reported on both sides of the 12-month window: 2024-12-31 (excluded, it is exactly DATEADD(MONTH,-12,AsOfDate)), 2025-01-01 (first day in), mid-year, 2025-12-31 (last day in) and 2026-01-01 (after AsOfDate). This trap is latent at the given AsOfDate of 2025-12-31: December and the December before both have 31 days, so DATEADD and add_months both return 2024-12-31. The rows pin the window boundaries, and the trap would only show with a reporting date like 2025-02-28, where add_months would move the lower bound to 2024-02-29.

Line 111: motor claims with lob_code 'mot', 'Mot' and 'MOT' on policies whose vehicle_reg is not in the Irish format ('ABC123'), plus one 'MOT' with a valid reg and one 'HOM' control. Under the CI collation all three case variants get invalid_reg_flag = 1; a plain Spark equality would give 0 for 'mot' and 'Mot' and change their score, band and reason.

Line 111: lob_code values 'MOT ' and 'MOT  ' (trailing spaces) on policies with an invalid reg 'XYZ999', next to a plain 'MOT' with the same invalid reg, a 'MOT' with a valid reg, and a 'HOM' control. SQL Server treats 'MOT ' = 'MOT' as true, so the padded rows get invalid_reg_flag = 1; a Spark equality would not flag them.

Motor claims whose vehicle_reg tests the LIKE character classes: '191-D-12345' (valid), '191-d-12345' (lowercase county, which [A-Z] matches under CI), '12-KY-9' (valid), 'ABC-123' (invalid, starts with letters), '1-D-123' (invalid, only one leading digit) and NULL (NOT LIKE on NULL is unknown, so no flag). A Spark LIKE would read the brackets as literal text and flag every non-NULL reg; a case-sensitive regex would flag the lowercase one.

Line 118: policy_number prefixes that differ from lob_code only in case: 'mot/2025/...' against 'MOT', 'Hom/2025/...' against 'HOM', and 'MOT/...' against lob 'mot'. Controls: an exact 'MOT' match and a real mismatch ('HOM/...' policy on a 'MOT' claim). Under CI the case-only rows get lob_mismatch_flag = 0; a case-sensitive Spark comparison would set it to 1. Regs are valid so only this flag varies.

Line 118: claims with lob_code 'MOT ', 'MOT  ' and 'HOM ' (trailing spaces) on policies whose numbers start with the matching 3-character prefix. Controls: an unpadded 'MOT' and a real mismatch. SQL Server ignores trailing spaces in <>, so the padded rows get lob_mismatch_flag = 0; Spark would set it to 1. Regs are valid, so a padded 'MOT ' that misses the motor check does not change the reg flag here.

Line 118: policy numbers in the standard 'LOB/yyyy/nnnnnn' form, so T-SQL SUBSTRING(x,0,4) returns the 3-character prefix ('MOT', 'HOM', 'TRV') and matching claims get lob_mismatch_flag = 0. Spark substring(x,0,4) returns 'MOT/' and would flag every one of them. Also included: real mismatches ('HOM/...' on a MOT claim, 'MOT/...' on a HOM claim) and a claim with no policy in the snapshot (NULL policy_number, so the <> is unknown and the flag is 0).

Line 152: loss dates with single-digit months and days (2025-01-02, 2025-03-07, 2025-09-09) and two-digit ones (2025-11-30, 2025-12-25), all in the reporting window. CONVERT style 112 gives an 8-character yyyymmdd loss_day_key; a plain cast would give a 10-character yyyy-MM-dd that does not fit CHAR(8).

Line 153: reported dates where day and month are both 12 or less (2025-03-04, 2025-04-05, 2025-12-01) and some where they are not (2025-07-25, 2025-10-31), so a day/month swap or a yyyy-MM-dd cast shows up in reason_text. Style 103 needs dd/MM/yyyy. One claim has a new customer, so both the ' - no indicators' and ' - NEWCUST' reason forms appear.

gates.reason: development run, approved by the agent (not a person's sign-off); warnings read: lineage agent notes: 1) The policy and customer joins (lines 88-92) are LEFT JOINs. They decide which policy and customer values get attached, but they never dr
warnings: lineage agent notes: 1) The policy and customer joins (lines 88-92) are LEFT JOINs. They decide which policy and customer values get attached, but they never drop a claim. They are recorded as filters at 0.85 confidence. If either join matches more than one row (e.g. duplicate policy_id within a snapshot, or a dw.dim_customer that is not one row per customer), a claim is repeated and the claim_id primary key is broken. 2) The join between #flags and #claims (line 162) is on claim_id, and both sides come from the same row set, so it neither filters nor adds rows. No separate edge is given for it. 3) Legacy behaviours the PySpark version must copy exactly: (a) early_notification_flag uses expiry_date, not inception_date as the comment says. inception_date is read into #claims but never used. (b) SUBSTRING(policy_number,0,4) returns only the first 3 characters (T-SQL start 0). If policy_number is NULL the <> test is UNKNOWN, so the flag is 0. (c) If vehicle_reg is NULL, NOT LIKE is UNKNOWN, so invalid_reg_flag is 0. If customer_since is NULL, new_customer_flag is 0. (d) The 'MOT' test and the lob mismatch test compare against the raw lob_code, not the upper-cased one. Under the default case-insensitive collation 'mot' still matches 'MOT', and trailing blanks are ignored. Spark compares case- and blank-sensitively, so its results can differ. (e) The LIKE pattern uses a T-SQL character class ([0-9], [A-Z]) and needs translating to a regex. (f) The reason_text date uses style 103 (dd/mm/yyyy). (g) If no snapshot is on or before @AsOfDate, @snapshot_date is NULL and every policy column is NULL.

warnings:
translator notes: 1) DATEADD(MONTH, -12, @AsOfDate) is worked out in Python using T-SQL's rule: the day is clamped only when the target month is shorter. For 2025-12-31 this gives 2024-12-31.
2) The snapshot date is found with an aggregate, then joined on. It is not collected. If no snapshot exists on or before the date, no policy rows match, which matches the legacy NULL @snapshot_date.
3) #flags is joined back to #claims on claim_id, just as the legacy code does. If claim_ids repeat (duplicate policy_id within a snapshot, or a dim_customer with more than one row per customer), rows multiply the same way. Legacy would then fail on the PK insert.
4) The LIKE pattern becomes the regex '(?is)^[0-9][0-9].*-[A-Z].*-[0-9]'. Only ASCII digits and letters match. Under the SQL_Latin1 collation, a non-ASCII character that sorts inside [0-9] or [A-Z] (for example superscript digits or accented letters) might match in legacy and not here. Only matters if such data exists.
5) The 'MOT' test and the LOB comparison use upper(rtrim()) on both sides. The stored lob_code is output as UPPER(RTRIM()), as in the legacy code.
6) loss_day_key is right-padded to CHAR(8). reason_text uses F.concat, so it is NULL if any part is NULL, like T-SQL +.
